Jeroboam II
jer-uh-BOH-um the SEK-und
proper noun (figure)
Hebrew Yarobam (H3379) — "may the people contend," "contender of the people," or possibly "the people will be many." From rib ("to strive, contend") + am ("people"). Named for the first king of the divided northern kingdom (Jeroboam I son of Nebat), under whom the golden-calf cult was established.

📖 Biblical Definition

Jeroboam II (c. 793 — 753 BC) was the thirteenth king of the northern kingdom of Israel (2 Kings 14:23-29), great-grandson of Jehu, who reigned forty-one years — the longest reign of any king in the divided monarchy north or south — and oversaw the greatest territorial expansion and material prosperity Israel had known since the days of Solomon. He recovered the coast from Hamath in the north to the Sea of the Arabah (Dead Sea) in the south (2 Kings 14:25), restoring the boundaries of the kingdom to what Solomon had ruled. Yet the canonical verdict assigns him only seven verses in 2 Kings 14:23-29 because his prosperity coincided with the most severe spiritual decay of the northern kingdom: "He did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD: he departed not from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin" (2 Kings 14:24). The fuller theological commentary on his reign is delivered through the prophets who ministered during it: Amos and Hosea. Amos was sent from Tekoa in Judah to Bethel in Israel during Jeroboam II's prosperity to denounce the wealthy women of Samaria as "kine of Bashan," the merchants who falsified the ephah and made the shekel great, the rulers who sold the righteous for silver and the poor for a pair of shoes, the luxurious houses of ivory in Samaria built on injustice. Hosea, an Israelite prophet himself, called the northern kingdom adulteress, harlot-Israel, the unfaithful wife of Yahweh. Jeroboam II's reign is the great Old Testament case study in prosperous-apostasy: the kingdom was militarily expanding, economically flourishing, and spiritually rotting all at once. He died (presumably) in his bed; his son Zechariah was assassinated after six months, and the northern kingdom's final forty years (753-722 BC) were a chaotic succession of coups, civil wars, and Assyrian invasions ending in the fall of Samaria.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Thirteenth king of the northern kingdom of Israel (c. 793-753 BC); great-grandson of Jehu; reigned 41 years (longest of any divided-monarchy king); restored Israel's borders to Solomonic extent; reign of great prosperity and great apostasy; ministry of Amos and Hosea fell within his reign.

JEROBOAM II, proper noun. Hebrew Yarobam (H3379) — "may the people contend," from rib ("strive") + am ("people").

Thirteenth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (c. 793-753 BC); great-grandson of Jehu (Jehu — Jehoahaz — Joash — Jeroboam II).

Reigned 41 years (longest of any king in either the divided-northern or divided-southern kingdom); restored Israel's borders from Hamath to the Sea of the Arabah (2 Kings 14:25).

Prophesied by the otherwise-unknown Jonah son of Amittai of Gath-hepher (2 Kings 14:25) — the same Jonah who later went to Nineveh.

Contemporary of Amos and Hosea; the great Old Testament case study in prosperous-apostasy.

📖 Key Scripture

2 Kings 14:25 — "He restored the coast of Israel from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain, according to the word of the LORD God of Israel, which he spake by the hand of his servant Jonah, the son of Amittai, the prophet, which was of Gath-hepher."

Amos 6:1-6 — "Woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria... That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock... That drink wine in bowls, and anoint themselves with the chief ointments: but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph."

Hosea 4:1-2 — "Hear the word of the LORD, ye children of Israel: for the LORD hath a controversy with the inhabitants of the land, because there is no truth, nor mercy, nor knowledge of God in the land. By swearing, and lying, and killing, and stealing, and committing adultery, they break out, and blood toucheth blood."

Amos 5:21-24 — "I hate, I despise your feast days, and I will not smell in your solemn assemblies... But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Jeroboam II is corrupted when his territorial expansion and economic prosperity are treated as canonical praise (they receive only seven verses precisely because Scripture is not impressed by them), when the prophetic indictment of Amos and Hosea is read in isolation from the kingly reign that occasioned it, or when his name's connection to the founder of the golden-calf cult (Jeroboam I) is overlooked.

expand to see more

Prosperity-as-blessing misreading. Jeroboam II is sometimes presented in popular histories as a kind of Solomon-redux of the northern kingdom — an expansionist, prosperous, internationally respected king. The text refuses this framing. Seven verses in 2 Kings 14:23-29 plus the entire books of Amos and Hosea ministering against his kingdom add up to one of the longest sustained prophetic indictments in the Old Testament. The prosperity itself is part of the indictment: it was built on falsified weights (Amos 8:5), oppression of the poor (Amos 2:6-7), drunken luxury (Amos 6:4-6), and continuing high-places worship at Bethel and Dan. The doctrinal lesson: economic flourishing in a covenant-rejecting nation is a sign of judgment ripening, not blessing.

Jonah-of-Gath-hepher cameo. 2 Kings 14:25 gives the curious detail that Jeroboam II's territorial expansion fulfilled the prophecy of "Jonah, the son of Amittai, the prophet, which was of Gath-hepher" — the same Jonah of the book of Jonah. This means that the prophet who would later be sent reluctantly to Nineveh had earlier prophesied prosperity for his own apostate northern kingdom. The juxtaposition is theologically rich: Jonah was happy to prophesy national prosperity to wicked Israel but resented being sent to prophesy mercy to Nineveh. The doctrinal point is uncomfortable: prophetic gifting does not guarantee prophetic willingness to bear God's compassion to outsiders.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Yarobam (H3379) — "may the people contend," from rib + am. Named for Jeroboam I, founder of the divided northern kingdom and of the golden-calf cult. Thirteenth king of Israel (c. 793-753 BC); 41-year reign.
